Beam has two core meanings as a verb. They feel different on the surface, but they share a beautiful common idea underneath: sending something outward with strength and brightness.
Meaning 1: To smile very widely and with great warmth

When a person beams, they are not just smiling — they are radiating joy from their whole face. It is a big, open, glowing smile that is impossible to hide. Think of the way a person's face completely lights up when they see someone they love after a long time, or when they hear the best news of their life. That is beaming.

Key qualities of beaming (vs. a regular smile):

  • It is full — the whole face is involved, not just the lips
  • It is involuntary — it bursts out naturally, you cannot really control it
  • It is directed — you usually beam at someone or with an emotion
  • It carries a sense of pride, happiness, or deep affection

Examples:

  • She beamed at her son as he walked across the stage to collect his diploma.
  • He beamed with pride when his team won the championship.
  • The little girl ran to her grandmother, who beamed and opened her arms wide.
  • "You did it!" she said, beaming.

Nuance — "beam at" vs. "beam with":

  • You beam at a person or thing — the smile is directed toward someone.
  • You beam with an emotion — you are full of that feeling and it shows.
    • She beamed at the camera. She beamed with joy.
Meaning 2: To send out or transmit something (light, signals, or information) in a focused direction

When a device, signal, light source, or broadcaster beams something, it is sending it out powerfully, directly, and in a targeted way — like a spotlight cutting through the dark. The idea is that the thing being sent is strong, focused, and travels in a clear direction, just like a beam of light.

Examples:

  • The satellite beamed the signal to millions of homes across the country.
  • The sun beamed through the curtains and woke her up.
  • The television station beamed the live match to over 50 countries.
  • A spotlight beamed down onto the singer on stage.
  • Scientists beamed a radio signal deep into space.

Notice the structure:

  • Something beams something → The satellite beamed the signal.
  • Something beams somewhere → Sunlight beamed through the clouds.
  • Something beams something somewhere → They beamed the broadcast across the world.

The key idea: You are not just sending something — you are sending it with focus and direction, like pointing a flashlight at a specific spot, not just turning on a lamp in a room.
The Shared Soul of Both Meanings

Here is what makes this word elegant: both meanings share the same core feeling of radiating something outward, brightly, and with direction.

  • A person who beams is radiating happiness outward through their face.
  • A satellite that beams a signal is radiating information outward through space.

In both cases, something bright and powerful is being sent out toward something or someone.

These are the most natural ways "beam" appears in real usage:

For the smiling meaning:

  • beam at someone (She beamed at him.)
  • beam with [emotion] (He beamed with delight / pride / happiness / pleasure.)
  • beam broadly (She beamed broadly and shook his hand.)
  • someone's face beams (His face beamed when he heard the news.)

For the transmitting meaning:

  • beam something to somewhere (beam the signal to Earth)
  • beam something across somewhere (beam the show across the nation)
  • beam down (The sun beamed down on us.)
  • beam through (Light beamed through the window.)
  • beam something live (The event was beamed live to millions.)

• Beam ≠ grin. A grin can be mischievous, sly, or cheeky. A beam is always warm, open, and joyful.
  • Beam ≠ transmit (in general). You only use "beam" when there is a sense of direction and focus — like a ray. You would not say "I beamed you an email." You would say "I sent you an email." But you would say "They beamed the broadcast directly to subscribers."
  • Beam ≠ gleam or glow (when used of light). Gleam and glow suggest softer, more diffuse light. A beam of light is directional and strong.

If you are unsure whether "beam" is the right word, ask yourself:

  • Is the smile full of warmth and big enough to light up someone's face? → Use beam.
  • Is the signal/light/broadcast being sent powerfully in a focused, directed way? → Use beam.

If yes to either, beam is your word.
